questions.q: What does retry_exponential_backoff=True change about how an Airflow task retries?
options: It disables retries entirely
It spaces retry attempts out with increasing delays instead of retrying immediately each time
It makes the task retry an unlimited number of times
It retries the entire DAG instead of just the failed task
questions.explain: Exponential backoff increases the delay between successive retry attempts, avoiding repeated immediate hits on a struggling upstream service.

questions.q: When does an Airflow task's on_failure_callback actually fire?
options: On every single attempt, including ones that will be retried
Only once the task has exhausted all of its retries and is genuinely failed
Before the task even starts running
Only when the entire DAG fails, never for an individual task
questions.explain: on_failure_callback fires once retries are exhausted, which is the right moment to alert a human since further automatic retries won't happen.

questions.q: Why is idempotency important for a task that might be retried?
options: It makes the task run faster
It ensures running the task once or several times (due to retries) leaves the system in the same correct final state, rather than duplicating or corrupting data
It prevents the task from ever failing
It is only relevant for tasks that read data, never for tasks that write data
questions.explain: Without idempotency, a retry after a partial failure can double-write or duplicate data; an idempotent task (e.g. using upsert or a fixed overwrite path) avoids this.

questions.q: What problem does checkpointing solve for a long training job?
options: It prevents the model from ever producing a wrong prediction
It lets training resume from a recent saved state after a crash, instead of restarting from the very beginning
It replaces the need for a model registry
It automatically fixes bugs in the training code
questions.explain: Periodically saving model and optimizer state means a crash late in training only loses the work since the last checkpoint, not everything.

questions.q: Why shouldn't a deterministic failure (e.g. a missing required column causing a KeyError) be retried the same way as a transient one?
options: Deterministic failures are actually more likely to succeed on retry
A deterministic failure will fail identically every time, so retrying it only delays alerting a human without fixing anything
Airflow does not allow retries on deterministic failures
Deterministic failures never need to be fixed
questions.explain: A deterministic bug produces the same failure on every attempt; retrying it wastes the retry delay without any chance of success, whereas a transient failure genuinely benefits from another attempt.
